form.2. SHORT COURSE DESCRIPTION: This course examines modern AI-native software development, where developers collaborate with increasingly capable coding agents. It covers how to define intent, provide effective context, structure development workflows, and coordinate AI tools. Students gain practical experience designing and evaluating agent-assisted software development processes.
form.3. TOPICS / CONTENT AREAS:
Treatment of this list: starting hypotheses — may add/drop/reorder with justification
A. AI-Native Development: AI-assisted coding, coding agents, developer workflows

B. Agentic Software Engineering: MCP, agent skills, tool use, context engineering

C. Specification & Planning: spec-driven development, requirements to executable specifications

D. Software Development Workflows: loop engineering, iterative development, software factories

E. Engineering Practice: automated testing, evaluation, deployment, reliability

F. Practical Development: hands-on coding, projects, emerging developer tools
form.4. COURSE INTENT:
Central question the course answers: How can software developers effectively
design and operate development workflows in which humans and AI agents
collaboratively build reliable software?

Pedagogical emphasis: Practical, workflow-oriented understanding through
hands-on development and experimentation.

This course should NOT become:
- A general introduction to AI or machine learning
- A traditional programming course
- A purely theoretical treatment of large language models

Programmes: B.Tech. CSE
Year: 3rd/4th year
Assumed background: Strong programming and software development fundamentals;
familiarity with advanced programming and basic software engineering concepts.

Available infrastructure: Student development machines, access to

form.12. ASSESSMENT PREFERENCES:
Preferred components: Practical assignments, hands-on coding exercises,
project-based evaluation, and a final project.

Components to avoid: none

AI-assisted development practices rather than primarily testing theory.

existence.reason: While CSE701 covers AI in software engineering from a data/research perspective, the new course focuses specifically on modern AI-native software development workflows, coding agents, tool use, and practical execution, making it a distinct practical offering.
existence.recommendation: Proceed as a distinct elective course.

overlaps.differentiation: CSE701 focuses broadly on mining software repositories and applying data/AI techniques to software engineering issues with a research orientation, whereas this course centers on hands-on AI-native development workflows, coding agents, and operational agent-assisted engineering.
CSE581 covers traditional and empirical systems analysis, design, and requirements engineering, whereas this course targets AI-native specification-driven development.
CSE582 focuses on product line engineering, maintenance, and re-engineering, which complements this course's focus on AI coding agents and automated workflows.
CSE594A emphasizes agentic reasoning for algorithmic and mathematical problem solving, whereas this course specializes in software development workflows and coding agents.

CSE201 provides foundational advanced programming and unit testing in Java, whereas this course builds upon those fundamentals to explore AI-assisted development and automated testing in agentic workflows.
AI501 is a core machine learning theory and methodology course, whereas this course applies software engineering practices to AI-native development.
CSE583 covers open source software development tools and practices, providing a foundation for collaborative engineering that complements AI-native developer workflows.
CSE665 covers the foundational principles and architecture of Large Language Models, whereas this course focuses on their practical application in software development workflows.

concerns.detail: The course duration is set to 50 weeks as per SC1, which is highly anomalous for a standard academic semester.

narrative.course_description: This course examines modern AI-native software development, focusing on how developers collaborate with coding agents. Designed for third- and fourth-year undergraduate students, the curriculum covers defining intent, structuring development workflows, and coordinating AI tools. Students learn to configure AI-assisted environments, translate high-level functional requirements into executable specifications, and analyze execution traces to diagnose agent-driven workflow failures. Additionally, they evaluate the correctness, reliability, and security risks of agent-generated code, and benchmark end-to-end software pipelines. The course is taught through three hours of lectures, one tutorial hour, and two practical lab hours per week, culminating in a hands-on project. Crucially, this is a practical, workflow-oriented engineering course rather than a general introduction to artificial intelligence, a traditional programming class, or a purely theoretical treatment of large language models.
narrative.sequencing_rationale: The course progresses logically from environment setup to pipeline integration. Students first configure AI-native environments (M1), building on foundational programming and unit testing prerequisites from CSE201. They then design specifications (M2) and trace workflow failures (M3). This enables them to perform automated testing and code reviews (M4), culminating in designing and benchmarking end-to-end pipelines (M5). This sequence ensures students master individual agent interactions before orchestrating complex, multi-agent software engineering pipelines.
narrative.assessment_rationale: The assessment mix balances theoretical understanding and practical application. Written exams (midsem 20%, endsem 30%) evaluate conceptual knowledge of context engineering and workflow tracing (CO2, CO3). Practical labs (10%) and assignments (20%) assess hands-on capabilities in environment configuration and automated testing (CO1, CO4). Finally, the term project (20%) requires students to design, evaluate, and benchmark a complete, end-to-end AI-native software pipeline (CO5), aligning with the highest cognitive levels of the course.
narrative.positioning_rationale: Unlike CSE201 (foundational programming) or CSE701 (research-oriented mining of software repositories), this course focuses on operational AI-native workflows. It differs from CSE581 (traditional systems analysis) and CSE582 (software product lines) by centering on specification-driven development using coding agents. While CSE594A targets algorithmic problem solving and AI501 covers core machine learning theory, this course applies software engineering practices to agentic workflows, complementing the open-source tools in CSE583 and LLM architectures in CSE665.
